paras: The threatened lynching of James Mills took place at West Chester, Pennsylvania, on November 20, 1888, when a hostile crowd met Mills, a Black man, as officers brought him to the Chester county prison. Mills was accused of assaulting and trying to drown Bertie Howard, an 11-year-old girl, near Paoli in September. He reached the jail unharmed and was given a hearing the same evening, and the papers dwelt mainly on his confession.

According to the West Chester Local, Mills, described as "a dark mulatto" from Connecticut who had been living with a white woman on a farm near Paoli, was accused of attacking the adopted daughter of farmer Isaac Beck of Tredyffrin as she walked home from school on September 28. The reports said he assaulted her in a field and threw her into a pond, leaving her for dead, before she reached a neighbor's house. Mills fled, and an "excited crowd of neighbors" searched the country for miles.

In early October residents of Tredyffrin met to raise money for the pursuit, and citizens of Malvern and Paoli offered a $250 reward. A Wilmington man found near Devon was arrested as Mills but released once he proved who he was.

Mills was arrested on the night of November 19 near Cranberry, New Jersey, by Officer Robert Jefferson of West Chester and Constable Jackson of Coatesville. The New York Sun's Hightstown correspondent instead placed the capture at a farmer's house near Englishtown, where Mills had worked on a threshing crew, and said two men taken for detectives brought him to the Hightstown depot.

When Mills arrived at West Chester on the afternoon of November 20, a "crowd of incensed men" lined the way from the railroad station to the jail, and the officers had to put him in a cab to get him through. The wire report said the hack was surrounded by a "hooting mob," and an Annapolis news brief added that "threats of lynching were heard." Meanwhile Isaac Beck went to the prison with a revolver, intending to shoot Mills on sight, but his friends, "partly by persuasion and partly by force," took the weapon from him before Mills was brought in.

That evening Squire Eupert gave Mills a partial hearing, at which Bertie Howard testified, and he was committed to jail again. Mills admitted the assault but said he was drunk, and the wire report said he denied trying to drown the girl. No report of a trial or sentence was found in the coverage.

Wilmington papers followed the case from the first report of the assault, reprinting the West Chester Local and reporting the pursuit and the reward. The arrest went out on the wire on November 20 and ran the next day in papers from Camden and New York to Memphis, St. Paul and Washington under headlines such as "A Flend Confesses His Crime" and "POOR BERTIE HOWARD." These reports called Mills a "brute," a "fiend" and a "would-be murderer," noted that he had lived with a white woman, and mentioned the hooting crowd only in passing.

The Delaware Gazette printed the fullest account, including Beck's armed visit and Mills' statement, and remarked that he "seemed perfectly unconcerned" while confessing. Some shorter versions, such as the Washington Evening Star's, left out the crowd altogether, and only the Annapolis brief spoke of lynching. No paper criticized the crowd or Beck.

Accounts of the capture differ: the West Chester reports name Cranberry and two Pennsylvania officers, while The Sun's Hightstown report names a farm near Englishtown and two unnamed men, and calls the foster father John rather than Isaac Beck. Mills' printed statement also departs from the wire summary, since in it he said he threw the girl into the water once and "Maybe I threw her in again."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of James Mills
bases: A crowd lined the way from the station to the jail and surrounded the hack carrying the accused man, and one report says 'threats of lynching were heard' (A6, A13, A14); no attack on him was reported.

Mills was not killed; he reached the Chester county prison and was given a hearing (A13). The episode is a threatened lynching only: a hooting crowd and, in one brief report, threats of lynching (A6, A14).

Several independent reports agree on the arrest, the jailing and the hostile crowd (A6, A7, A13); the explicit lynching threats rest on the Annapolis brief alone (A14), and Beck's revolver on A13 and A14.
